newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish court allows appeal on "dirty war" files.
newsitem.headline: Spanish court allows appeal on "dirty war" files.

text.p: Spain's Supreme Court moved a step closer on Friday towards opening secret files on a 1980s "dirty war" against Basque separatists which could implicate former prime minister Felipe Gonzalez.
The court admitted part of an appeal by victims' families against the current conservative government's decision to keep the military intelligence documents secret.

The appeal, if successful, would allow judges to deepen their investigation into allegations that Socialist officials oversaw a death squad campaign against Basque rebels which killed 27 people between 1983 and 1987.

Justice Minister Margarita Mariscal de Gante said in a radio interview the government "will have to comply with this order" if the Supreme Court rules the papers must be declassified. Gonzalez on Thursday denied that state terrorism ever took place, provoking a fierce backlash from other political leaders.

"Clearly, there hadn't been state terrorism in Spain," the former premier told a Spanish radio interviewer. "If there had been state terrorism, there wouldn't have been 900 victims from security forces, armed forces and civilians and 28 (sic)...from supposed terrorists; the numbers would have been inverted."
The former administration refused to comply with a judicial order to hand over the files, citing reasons of state security.
After considering the issue for three months, the new government of Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar decided in August to keep the documents under lock and key, rejecting court requests for access.
The government's Basque allies have accused it of striking a secret deal with its Socialist predecessors to cover up the campaign against ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom).
"There is an iron pact at work here between certain (political) parties," Inaki Ansagasti, spokesman for the moderate Basque Nationalist Party (PNV), said in August.
The Socialists' first interior minister is on trial in the Supreme Court, accused of creating and funding the self-styled GAL (Anti-terrorist Liberation Groups) that waged the illegal campaign.
Gonzalez himself has avoided any court appearances in the scandal that helped force an early election last March and helped put the PP in power.
The Supreme Court has yet to decide if the former premier will appear in court - either as a witness or a suspect.
